problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
### Summary  

**a. Verdict:**  
I have successfully solved the problem. The minimum number of rectangular tiles required is  

\[
\boxed{4048}.
\]

**b. Method Sketch:**  

1. **Permutation representation.**  
   The uncovered squares form a permutation matrix: there is a bijection  
   \(\sigma:\{1,\dots ,n\}\to\{1,\dots ,n\}\) (\(n=2025\)) such that the unique uncovered
   square in row \(i\) lies in column \(\sigma(i)\).  

2. **Decomposition into left and right regions.**  
   For each row \(i\) set  

   \[
   a_i=\sigma(i)-1\qquad(\text{number of covered cells to the left of the hole}),\qquad   
   b_i=n-\sigma(i)\qquad(\text{number of covered cells to the right}).
   \]

   The set of covered cells splits into two disjoint parts  

   \[
   L=\{(i,j):1\le j\le a_i\},\qquad   
   R=\{(i,j):\sigma(i)+1\le j\le n\}.
   \]

3. **Lower bound \(2n-2\).**  
   Because \(\sigma\) is a permutation, the numbers \(\{a_i\}\) are a permutation of
   \(\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}\); exactly \(n-1\) of them are positive and they are all
   distinct.  

   *Left region.*  
   For each row with \(a_i>0\) consider the right‑most covered cell \((i,a_i)\).
   The column indices \(a_i\) are pairwise distinct.  
   Suppose a single axis‑parallel rectangle contained two such cells,
   say \((i,a_i)\) and \((i',a_{i'})\) with \(a_i<a_{i'}\).  
   Then the rectangle’s column interval contains the column \(a_i+1\); but
   column \(a_i+1\) is precisely the uncovered square in row \(i\), a
   contradiction.  
   Hence each \((i,a_i)\) must belong to a different rectangle, forcing at least
   \(n-1\) rectangles to cover \(L\).

   *Right region.*  
   The left‑most covered cell of row \(i\) in \(R\) is \((i,\sigma(i)+1)\).
   The column numbers \(\sigma(i)+1\) are also pairwise distinct, and the same
   argument shows that at least \(n-1\) rectangles are needed for \(R\).

   Since \(L\) and \(R\) are disjoint, any tiling of the whole board needs at
   least  

   \[
   (n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2
   \]

   rectangles.

4. **Construction attaining the bound.**  
   Choose the identity permutation \(\sigma(i)=i\) (the uncovered squares are the
   diagonal cells \((i,i)\)). Then  

   \[
   a_i=i-1,\qquad b_i=n-i .
   \]

   *Covering \(L\).*  
   For each column \(k\) with \(1\le k\le n-1\) place the vertical rectangle  

   \[
   T_k=\{(i,k):k+1\le i\le n\},
   \]

   which is a \((n-k)\times1\) tile.  
   Because \(a_i=i-1\ge k\) exactly when \(i\ge k+1\), the cell \((i,k)\) belongs
   to \(T_k\) iff it is a covered cell of \(L\). The rectangles \(T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}\)
   are pairwise disjoint and together cover every cell of \(L\).  
   Thus \(L\) is tiled with \(n-1\) rectangles.

   *Covering \(R\).*  
   For each column \(k\) with \(n-k+1\le k\le n\) (equivalently \(k= n-j\) with
   \(1\le j\le n-1\)) place the vertical rectangle  

   \[
   S_j=\{(i,n-j+1):1\le i\le n-j\},
   \]

   a \((n-j)\times1\) tile.  
   Since \(b_i=n-i\ge j\) exactly when \(i\le n-j\), the cell \((i,n-j+1)\) is a
   covered cell of \(R\) precisely when it lies in \(S_j\). The rectangles
   \(S_1,\dots,S_{n-1}\) are disjoint and cover all of \(R\).

   Altogether we have \((n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2\) non‑overlapping rectangles, and each
   row and each column contains exactly one uncovered square (the diagonal).

5. **Conclusion.**  
   The lower bound \(2n-2\) is achievable, so it is optimal. For \(n=2025\),

   \[
   2n-2 = 2\cdot2025-2 = 4050-2 = 4048 .
   \]

Hence the minimum number of tiles required is \(\boxed{4048}\).
